story_text.value:
Something the HN crowd might appreciate.

This website will open (on the client side) pretty much any file you throw at it.

412 file formats are supported: every raw camera format, obscure video/audio codecs, 3D files, virtualized images, IC designs, Photoshop/Coreldraw designs and much more.

You can also export most of them to common formats: PNG for images, MP4 for videos, CSV for data, etc. You can trim video and audio files when you export them.

There’s around 100 MB of WASM decoders that are loaded dynamically, keeping the website fast and snappy.

Any file format you'd like to see supported?

story_text.value:
Hi everyone. I've been building Imza for the last three months. It's yet another coding agent. I know there are a dozen have been posted here. But I believe this one is different enough to have a place here.

It has three explicit modes: plan, build and review. Plan mode allows you to draft a spec document together with the agent. Both you and the agent can edit the document until everything is clear. Build mode takes the plan and implements it. Review mode provides you a code review tool. You can annotate things you want to change in the code and send them as revision to the plan mode.

It's entirely written in C++, requires no account, supports 50+ providers including OpenAI subscriptions or local models. Imza supports MCP, skills and instruction files out of the box and uses 8-11MB RAM at startup.

One of the biggest differentiator is the Lua engine. What I did differently here is agent receives only one tool, that allows the LLM to execute Lua scripts. I then passed C++ methods as Lua bindings that the agent can execute. So model can orchestrate multiple bindings in one call. Each binding passes through a permission layer. Since Lua is the only way to interact with the filesystem, imza can monitor and control the model's behavior.

I'd love to hear your feedback. Thanks

Website: https://imza.run

Source: https://github.com/umutsevdi/imza

story_text.value:
Update to an earlier Show HN. KuralHub is a catalog of speech emotion datasets for the 70 most widely spoken languages, with benchmark results for 11 pretrained speech models on 33 of those datasets. Version 1.0 adds:

- A searchable catalog with one page per language. Each of the 90 datasets lists its emotion labels, size, licence, access link and citation. - All 363 benchmark runs as downloadable CSV and JSON, with the logs for each run. - The published paper (Interspeech 2026), and code that runs on current PyTorch and Transformers. - A short form for suggesting a missing dataset or a model to benchmark.

The most practical finding: the right model depends on the language. Whisper had the best average, but HuBERT came out on top for nine languages, bigger checkpoints did not help, and Tamil, Telugu and Kannada were hard for every model.

25 of the 70 languages still have no known emotional speech dataset, including Sinhala, Nepali, Hausa and Yoruba.

Catalog: https://aaivu.github.io/KuralHub/datasets.html Results: https://aaivu.github.io/KuralHub/benchmark.html What changed: https://github.com/aaivu/KuralHub/releases/tag/v1.0.0 Paper: https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2026/thavarasa26_in...

Suggestions for missing datasets are welcome, especially for those 25 languages, and so are new languages beyond the current 70.

story_text.value:
Hi all,

I switched from wallabag to readeck and was missing a way to sync articles to my kobo device, which was previously done by wallabako[1].

I forked that project, discarded some features (support for KOReader/Plato, on-screen progress etc.), extended testing and documentation to end up with Kobodeck, which after some months of use feels stable enough to share.

This could be useful for people who only want to read articles on their kobo, there is at least one more full-featured solution being developed that can do much more than that[2].

Happy to receive any feedback or suggestions about this.

[1] https://gitlab.com/anarcat/wallabako [2] https://bandarlabs.github.io/Cobalt/
